title: Manifest OS Raises $60M Series A at $750M Valuation to Scale the AI-Native Law Firm Model
author: Richard Tromans · citybiz staff

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s work-redesign thesis and materially extends it with a concrete AI-native operating model: centralized workflows and AI-trained support staff under attorney supervision, coupled with embedded AI and outcomes-based pricing. It illustrates institutional redesign rather than tool procurement, although its scale, access and alignment benefits remain strategic claims without comparative performance or client-outcome evidence.
qs: Manifest OS recruits paralegals, admins and legal writers, and trains them to become AI-proficient while handling client intake, business development, quality assurance, billing and collections, all under attorney supervision.

kp.k: Funding supports expansion of an AI-native service delivery model
kp.d: The April 2026 coverage reports a $60 million Series A at a $750 million valuation, backed by Menlo Ventures, Kleiner Perkins, First Round Capital and, in citybiz's account, Quiet Capital. Planned uses include platform development and expansion beyond immigration law. The description of this as the largest legal-technology Series A is explicitly the company's claim.
qs: Manifest OS, the company building AI-native law firms designed around fixed-fee pricing and automated legal workflows, has **raised $60 million in Series A funding at a $750 million** valuation, marking what it says is the largest Series A round in legal technology to date.
The capital will be used to expand Manifest OS's platform, scale its AI-native law firm model and support broader adoption across legal practice areas beyond its initial focus on immigration law.

kp.k: Shared brand, software and operations underpin affiliated law firms
kp.d: Manifest OS describes a three-component structure: firms share the Manifest Law brand, an end-to-end AI-native platform and centralized operational infrastructure. The proposed mechanism for scaling is standardization of pricing, service quality and client experience alongside shared support functions, rather than software deployment alone.
qs: All firms operate under the unified Manifest Law brand, creating a consistent standard for transparent pricing, service quality, and client experience.

Manifest OS provides an AI-native platform that acts as a single end-to-end solution for client communications, attorney and client collaboration, legal research, document drafting, billing and reporting.
Manifest OS provides centralized operational infrastructure that allows for Manifest-branded firms to achieve the scale of a large law firm.

kp.k: Fixed-fee pricing replaces hourly incentives in newly built firms
kp.d: CEO Dan Mishin presents rebuilding the law-firm business model as necessary for outcomes-based pricing and broader access to high-quality services. He says Manifest OS deliberately avoids selling software to incumbent firms because their compensation incentives favor billing more hours, instead partnering with lawyers to establish AI-native practices. Citybiz describes these as fixed-fee or outcomes-based models; Artificial Lawyer reports opposition to billable hours.
qs: We made the hard choice to not sell our AI software to existing law firms who are often beholden to billing customers more hours as a means to better compensation.
Instead, we partner with forward-thinking lawyers to help them become market leaders in their respective practice areas, with AI at their core from day zero.
Instead, Manifest OS partners with attorneys to build firms that are structured around AI-driven efficiency and fixed-fee or outcomes-based pricing models from the outset.

To truly shift the market to outcomes-based pricing and to democratize access to high-quality legal services for clients, we needed to rethink the entire business model of a law firm from the ground up

kp.k: Investor frames pricing reform as aligning lawyers and clients
kp.d: David Schellhase, a Manifest investor and former general counsel, argues from his corporate legal experience that hourly billing creates friction for both buyers and providers. He presents Manifest's model as aligning companies' demand for predictable fees and speed with lawyers' desire to deliver results rather than justify hours. This is an investor's assessment, not a reported comparative study.
qs: I've spent my career as a general counsel for some of the largest tech companies in the world and seen firsthand how the billable hour model creates friction on both sides of the table.
Companies want fee transparency, predictability, and speed. Lawyers want to focus on delivering results, not justifying billable hours.
Manifest OS's model and use of advanced technology align those interests in a way the traditional system simply doesn't.

kp.k: AI assists workflows while attorneys retain final approval
kp.d: The company describes human-supervised agents embedded in legal workflows as eliminating non-legal administration and standardizing quality, freeing lawyers for strategic advice and client relationships. Citybiz specifically reports attorney final review and approval of AI-assisted document preparation and case workflows, alongside HR and recruiting integrations and real-time case visibility. The described model therefore retains human responsibility rather than relying directly on autonomous output.
qs: Human-supervised AI agents are embedded directly into legal workflows, eliminating non-legal administrative work and standardizing quality.
That frees lawyers to focus on delivering a high-touch, human experience and strategic counsel that technology cannot replace.
AI tools are used to assist with document preparation and case workflows, while attorneys retain final review and approval responsibilities.
The system integrates with client HR and recruiting platforms and provides real-time visibility into case status, timelines and documentation.

kp.k: Centralized support roles receive AI training under attorney supervision
kp.d: Manifest OS says it recruits and trains paralegals, administrators and legal writers to become AI-proficient, while centralizing intake, business development, quality assurance, billing and collections under attorney supervision. Its stated division of labor reserves legal work and client advocacy for lawyers and assigns the operational infrastructure to Manifest OS.
qs: Manifest OS recruits paralegals, admins and legal writers, and trains them to become AI-proficient while handling client intake, business development, quality assurance, billing and collections, all under attorney supervision.
Lawyers at Manifest OS-powered law firms focus on legal work and client advocacy, while Manifest OS provides the back-office engine to power the practice.

kp.k: Arizona ABS framework hosts the initial immigration practice
kp.d: The first Manifest Law firm was incubated in business immigration under Arizona's alternative business structure framework. Artificial Lawyer identifies Mishin as a nonlawyer CEO. The document describes this regulatory setting for the initial practice without detailing how expansion into other practice areas would be structured.
qs: Manifest OS incubated its first law firm in the business immigration market under the "Manifest Law" brand as part of the Arizona ABS program.
And CEO **Dan Mishin** – who is not a lawyer and is understood not to know any secret legal handshakes – commented:

kp.k: Company reports immigration scale, selectivity and operational improvements
kp.d: According to company figures carried by citybiz, the first firm has handled more than 3,000 client engagements and works with over 100 immigration attorneys and co-counsel partners. It reports accepting fewer than 1% of more than 5,000 attorney applicants, faster responses and visa approval rates above national benchmarks. The document supplies no numerical response-time or approval-rate comparison or measurement period.
qs: According to the company, the first AI-native firm has handled more than 3,000 client engagements and works with over 100 immigration attorneys and co-counsel partners.
Manifest OS said the platform has contributed to operational improvements including faster client response times and higher visa approval rates compared to national benchmarks.
The company also reported strong demand from legal professionals, noting that fewer than 1% of more than 5,000 attorney applicants were accepted into its network.

kp.k: Investors anticipate value shifting toward AI-native legal services
kp.d: Citybiz frames the investment as part of a shift from point solutions toward platforms restructuring service delivery, placing it against an estimated roughly $400 billion US legal market dominated by time-based billing. Kleiner Perkins's Ilya Fushman predicts value concentration in AI-native services; Menlo Ventures's Shawn Carolan anticipates major improvements in economics and speed. These are market framing and investor expectations, rather than demonstrated market-wide outcomes.
qs: Investor interest in Manifest OS reflects a broader shift in legal technology, where venture capital is increasingly focused on AI-driven platforms that go beyond point solutions and aim to restructure core service delivery models.
The legal services market in the United States is estimated to be worth roughly $400 billion, with the majority of spend still tied to time-based billing structures.
Selling AI-native services is where a lot of the industry's value will be concentrated, and Manifest OS is uniquely positioned to build a category-defining market leader
It was clear to us that the right team, building with AI at their core, would offer step-function improvements in both economics and speed.

kp.k: Broader disruption depends on expansion beyond immigration
kp.d: Richard Tromans interprets Manifest OS's shared infrastructure as capable of supporting multiple practice areas and reiterates Artificial Lawyer's prediction of NewMod growth in 2026. He qualifies the prospect of major legal-market disruption by saying Manifest must enter many more higher-value areas beyond immigration. This is author commentary about future potential, distinct from the company's reported initial operations.
qs: And, as AL predicted at the end of last year: NewMods are going large in 2026!
I.e. this seems to be saying that they could branch out into other areas of the law.
Of course, if they're going to rock the legal world, they'll need to move into many more higher value areas beyond immigration law.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Manifest OS claims that an integrated AI-native firm model can automate administration, standardize quality and let lawyers concentrate on strategic advice and client relationships.
pts.d: In the company explanation reproduced by Richard Tromans, shared branding, an end-to-end software platform and centralized operations jointly enable Manifest-branded firms to achieve large-firm scale. The claimed mechanism is human-supervised AI embedded in workflows, supported by AI-proficient staff. This is augmentation with attorney supervision, not unsupervised replacement of lawyers. Citybiz additionally reports company claims of faster client responses and visa approval rates above national benchmarks.

pts.k: Dan Mishin and David Schellhase claim that building firms around AI from inception enables a shift away from hourly billing toward predictable, results-oriented pricing.
pts.d: Mishin frames the change as a redesign of the law-firm business model rather than software sales to incumbent firms, whose compensation incentives he describes as tied to billing more hours. Citybiz describes fixed-fee or outcomes-based pricing; these are presented as alternatives to hourly billing, not necessarily identical arrangements. Schellhase, a Manifest investor and former general counsel, argues that the model aligns clients' demands for transparency, predictability and speed with lawyers' desire to focus on results. Mishin also claims an ambition to democratize access, without specifying underserved populations or measuring unmet legal need.

pts.k: Investors predict substantial economic value and improvements in speed from AI-native legal services; Tromans predicts growth in AI-first firm models.
pts.d: Kleiner Perkins managing partner Ilya Fushman predicts that much industry value will concentrate in selling AI-native services and positions Manifest OS as a prospective market leader. Menlo Ventures partner Shawn Carolan predicts major economic and speed improvements from the right team building around AI. Tromans treats the funding as investor confidence in the NewMod approach and reiterates his prediction of growth in 2026. Citybiz characterizes the investment as part of a broader shift from point software solutions toward restructuring service delivery. These are investor and author forecasts or interpretations, distinct from reported operating results.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists of company-reported operating figures and benchmark comparisons, a funding event, professional experience and anecdotal interest in new firms.
pts.d: Both accounts report a $60 million Series A at a $750 million valuation. Citybiz attributes to the company more than 3,000 client engagements, a network of over 100 immigration attorneys and co-counsel partners, and acceptance of fewer than 1% of more than 5,000 attorney applicants. These figures describe activity, network size and recruitment selectivity, rather than directly measuring AI's effects. Faster responses and higher visa approval rates are company-reported, with no numerical improvement, named benchmark, comparison period or methodology supplied. Schellhase invokes his general-counsel experience to support the billing-friction claim and is identified as an investor. Tromans offers three recent inquiries about forming AI-first firms as an anecdotal yardstick. Investor predictions are supported by their stated assessments, not quantified economic or speed results.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Present operating claims concern business immigration; expansion is prospective, while Tromans specifically forecasts NewMod growth in 2026.
pts.d: The Artificial Lawyer account is dated 28 April 2026. Reported engagement totals and performance claims concern the initial business-immigration firm, without a stated measurement period. The initial launch operates under Arizona's alternative business structure framework. Attorney supervision and final review remain conditions of the delivery model. Funding is intended to support entry into additional practice areas and further platform development, but no expansion timetable is supplied. Tromans qualifies the prospect of broader disruption by saying Manifest must enter more higher-value areas beyond immigration. Fushman's value-concentration prediction and Carolan's improvement prediction have no explicit deadline; Carolan conditions improvement on the right team building with AI at its core.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate affected groups are business-immigration clients, participating lawyers and support staff; prospective effects extend to other practices and incumbent hourly-billing firms.
pts.d: Corporate clients, including HR and recruiting teams, are promised transparent pricing, faster service and visibility into cases. Lawyers in Manifest-powered firms are described as focusing on legal work, advocacy and relationships while retaining responsibility for review and approval. Paralegals, administrators and legal writers are recruited and trained in AI rather than expressly forecast to disappear. Manifest OS supplies software, brand and centralized operations to affiliated firms instead of selling software to traditional firms. Incumbent firms are the model's competitive target because of their hourly-billing incentives. Mishin's broader access claim does not identify effects on the civil justice gap or particular underserved groups.
